newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgians would back child victims political party.
newsitem.headline: Belgians would back child victims political party.

text.p: Over half of Belgium's French- speaking population would vote for a new political party backed by the parents of victims in the country's paedophile and murder scandal if one were formed, a newspaper poll showed on Sunday.

Weekly Dimanche Matin asked 600 southern Belgians whether they would back a so-called "White March" party, if one sprang up following a rally in Brussels last October for missing children which was attended by quarter of a million people.

Wearing white to symbolise innocence and hope, the marchers filed through the capital in support of the child victims' families and to show their disgust at the law and order system which had allowed the paedophile gang to go undetected.

The poll - carried out by Sobemap Marketing and the French-language newspaper - showed 56 percent of those questioned would either "definitely" or "probably" vote for such a White March party at the next elections if it existed.
Five percent had no opinion, and the rest would not vote for the party. The survey was carried out between December 27 and 30, and had an error margin of four percent, the paper said.

Four girls' bodies have been discovered, around the southern city of Charleroi, since the scandal erupted in August when two others were rescued alive from a house owned by chief suspect in the scandal, convicted rapist Marc Dutroux. They had both been sexually abused.

The parents of the dead girls, who led the White March, have campaigned actively for answers from the authorities to the police and judicial bungling which marked the investigation into their daughters' disappearances.

Together with the families of 13 other abducted children, they have also called repeatedly for law changes to prevent such horrors being repeated and to make the legal system more accessible to ordinary people and understanding of victims.

Paul Marchal, the father of one of the dead girls told Germany's Bild am Sonntag newspaper last month that a "White Party" would be formed if Belgian Prime minster Jean-Luc Dehaene did not establish concrete laws soon.
However the fathers of eight-year-old victims Melissa Russo and Julie Lejeune told Belgian television on Sunday that for them there was no question of creating a political party.
"We can bring more pressure to bear by remaining as parents than by forming a political party," Gino Russo said.
"What we hope is that the existing parties will review their policies," Jean-Denis Lejeune added.
The parents have already won sympathy and pledges of judicial and police reform from the government which is eager to restore shattered public confidence in the system.
